Article Title: Decoding the business of bringing Brazil, Uruguay, Panama to India for football friendlies
Article Text:
Soccer Football - International Friendly - India v Brazil - Salt Lake Stadium, Kolkata, India - October 3, 2026 Brazil's Vinicius Junior in action with India's Ryan Williams REUTERS/Sahiba Chawdhary

New Delhi:

Who pays for the spectacle?

Supporters cheer for their teams during the International Friendly football match between India and Brazil at Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan, in Kolkata. (ANI)

Brazilian player Pedro (19) celebrates after his goal during an international friendly football match between India and Brazil at the Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan (Salt Lake Stadium) in Kolkata. (PTI)

The problem with selling a Brazil match

India and Brazil football players during the international friendly match at the Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan (Salt Lake Stadium) in Kolkata. (PTI)

A delegation of the Brazilian Football Confederation and others inspect the field at Salt lake Stadium, also known as Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan (PTI Photo/Swapan Mahapatra)

Why planning matters more than ticket prices

Brazil supporters during the FIFA friendly between India and Brazil at the Salt Lake Stadium in Kolkata. (Image: PTI)

Kohana, her husband and four boys travelled from Chennai to Kolkata for the India vs Brazil game. (Image: Tanuj Lakhina/TimesofIndia.com)

Angry fans vandalised the Salt Lake Stadium, alleging poor management during Argentine footballer Lionel Messi's G.O.A.T India Tour 2025 in Kolkata. (ANI)

Why government backing matters

I think there's a lot of negative news around (Indian) football. So as long as that's there, the appetite will be limited. But I think this one event will change the appetite for future events. Anuj Kichlu

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bringing Brazil to India was not just about getting one of football's biggest names to play a match. It was about negotiating with federations, securing the right venue, arranging travel and accommodation, ensuring security, maintaining the pitch and, ultimately, figuring out who will pay for it all.The financial stakes are substantial. An international friendly involving a World Cup nation can cost at least Rs 10 crore, while staging a match involving one of the biggest teams could push the bill to Rs 100 crore, according to Anuj Kichlu, director and CEO of Best of You, which helped facilitate India's friendlies against Panama, Brazil and Uruguay "It would happen depending on the team. But an international friendly of a World Cup nation kind of friendly will not come under 10 crores," Kichlu told TimesofIndia.com after the three friendlies in Bengaluru and Kolkata."I'm saying you take the cost of the team, the cost of their travel, the cost of the stadium, event, and that. So the lowest you'll get a World Cup team is at Rs 10 crores, and the highest it'll cost is even 100 crores for one match, depending on the team."The figures, he explained, cover considerably more than the fee for securing a team's appearance."It's appearance, logistics, flights, hotels, securities, player's safety, police, in-stadium branding, event management, insurances.Everything would be covered," he explained.The challenge, therefore, is not simply to bring a marquee team to India. It is to make the economics of the event work in a market where the appetite for international football is still developing.There is no single business model for staging an international friendly. The financial structure depends on who initiates the event and what they hope to achieve.A private promoter may organise a match with the expectation of recovering the investment through ticket sales, sponsorships and broadcast rights. A football federation, meanwhile, may be driven by sporting objectives, including giving its national team exposure against stronger opposition.In the case of India's recent friendlies, the AIFF approached the Spain-headquartered Best of You to help bring international teams to the country. They acted as a match agent, negotiating with the visiting federations and coordinating arrangements for their participation. Commercialisation, including ticketing and broadcasting, was handled separately by the AIFF and its agencies.Kichlu was clear about the distinction."Yeah, they engaged agencies for sponsorship. They engaged agencies for ticketing. They had security agencies for private security. They engaged with several different vendors, 5-6 different vendors for different roles," said Kichlu, who leads the company's India office.They, meanwhile, are not necessarily the party carrying the event's commercial risk."It's two federations only, and we come in as match agents. So we are not actually a party on the contract, but we are match agents on the contract," he said on how the agreement is drawn.He explained that the agent's responsibilities included areas such as insurance and cancellation, rather than the commercialisation of the event.That separation is important. While the agent helps secure the teams and ensure contractual obligations are met, the federation and its commercial partners must work out whether the event can generate enough revenue to justify the expenditure.Brazil was the centrepiece of the three friendly series, for which India opted against playing the FIFA ASEAN Cup , selected for its substantial fan following in India, especially in Kolkata. Panama was brought in as a preparatory opponent, while Uruguay was added later when an opportunity arose to secure the team at a comparatively favourable price during their tour of Japan and South Korea.But the appeal of a famous team does not automatically translate into a commercially successful event.Kichlu believes the market for international football in India has potential, although negative publicity surrounding the sport has affected confidence among both spectators and sponsors."I think there's a lot of negative news around (Indian) football. So as long as that's there, the appetite will be limited. But I think this one event will change the appetite for future events."He said the matches had generated interest in future fixtures, despite the commercial challenges."So already we are getting inquiries for future matches and stuff in India because this one was successful, other than commercially. If you see everything on the ground was quite successful."For sponsors, however, interest alone is insufficient. Brands want measurable evidence that an event can deliver an audience and provide value for their investment."Not only fans, even I'd say sponsors obviously are reluctant to associate with something if they don't have numbers and backing, right? So when you go to someone and say you're sponsoring a Brazil match and they ask you for data of another big match in India, you don't have a match to go by," he stated.The lack of comparable events makes it difficult to establish what sponsors should expect from a major international friendly. Television ratings, digital views and stadium attendance can offer useful indicators, but they need to be interpreted carefully.Kichlu pointed out that even television figures can be difficult to assess without knowing how long viewers watched. Digital views, too, do not necessarily reflect sustained engagement. The recent elation with viewership of the Indian Super League (ISL) is an example of keeping caution.The friendlies, meanwhile, could therefore serve as a reference point for future commercial decisions."So decisions in the future will be made based on these 3 matches and the UK tour (Unity Cup against Nigeria and Zimbabwe) and stuff like that," said Kichlu.For Indian football, the ability to turn those experiences into reliable audience data could be as important as securing the next marquee opponent.The attendance at the Salt Lake Stadium for the friendlies against Brazil and Uruguay raised eyebrows. 51,402 came through the gates for the Brazil game and 37,307 for the contest against Uruguay. Different reasons have been suggested for the less-than-expected turnout. Kichlu believes the marketing window and the timing of the event played a significant role."I think the marketing for the match was pretty late, to be honest, because with the kind of prices they're charging for those tickets, it means it's not that people aren't willing to pay it," he said."I think it just needs more planning because people will dedicate budgets to this compared to something else, and I would say a lot of people would have committed money somewhere else," he continued.The short lead time also limited the opportunity to attract fans from outside Kolkata."And with a 2-3 week window only, people would have made other plans to travel to other places. Being a long weekend also, I would say a lot of the people from Bombay, Delhi, Bangalore, stuff like that, would have made other plans to go on holidays in other places."His argument is that a match involving Brazil should not be marketed only to the city hosting it. It has the potential to draw spectators from across India, but doing so requires advance planning."But if they had, say, a 2-and-a-half, 3-month notice, they would have probably planned towards this.""I think the disappointing thing was that the number of people from across India who traveled for the match was low compared to what you would expect for this kind of a match."Concerns about safety following the earlier Lionel Messi event in Kolkata had, he said, made some parents cautious about bringing their children to another high-profile football event."I think we have to work more on the family experience and obviously giving more time and with that, it'll work."He does not believe ticket prices and it coming two weeks before Durga Puja explain the lower attendance."To be honest, the pricing of the tickets, I've researched all over Asia and even countries who are as far as India, and people are willing to pay this and much more for these kind of matches.""So I don't think it's that much of the ticketing price. I think it's the people who are willing to pay for these tickets are the ones who didn't come to the stadium," he reasoned.If ticketing and sponsorship alone cannot guarantee a return, who should pay for the difference?Kichlu believes government support can be crucial when a country is trying to establish itself as a destination for major international football."I think government should play more of a role, right? If they want to bring these events, like, any state government wants to bring these kind of events to their state, they'd have to also pitch in resources. That's exactly why Brazil went to Australia.""The two matches were funded by the Queensland state government. It was part of their objective to promote the state internationally."The investment, in such cases, is not necessarily intended to be recovered entirely through ticket sales. Governments may see international sporting events as a way to promote a destination, generate publicity and build the infrastructure and reputation required to host larger events.Kichlu said the economics in established football markets are different for such friendlies because ticketing and broadcast revenues are more predictable."In Europe, you can take a team and you can make it commercially viable because the market is there, people are willing to pay it."In emerging markets, he argued, the commercial foundations are not yet as secure."And if you don't do that, I don't think these events are economical to organise like it is in Europe, where you have a set ticket price you can charge. You know what broadcast rights you'll get. You know what sponsorship you'll get. Everything is starting at a base level. So you have to have backing," he finished.
Article Summary: An international friendly involving a World Cup nation can cost at least Rs 10 crore. Staging a match involving one of the biggest teams could push the bill to Rs 100 crore. Financial structure depends on who initiates the event and what they hope to achieve.

Argentina's Lionel Messi celebrates after scoring his side���s third goal from the penalty spot during his final match for the national team, a soccer friendly against Benin, in Buenos Aires, Argentina, Tuesday, Oct.6, 2026. AP/PTI(AP10_08_2026_000008B)

Messi is not the first footballer honoured by science

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Neotrichia pelei

A sage plant discovered in the Peruvian Andes has become the sixth species named after Lionel Messi , extending a record already shared by a lizard, spider, fossil brachiopod, condor and fungus. The newly describedcarries Argentina’s familiar blue and white colours in its flowers, but the tribute comes with a troubling detail: researchers have classified the plant as endangered.is a sage species endemic to the Andes of central and southern Peru, where it grows on rocky, arid slopes between 2,000 and 2,400 metres above sea level. It belongs to the mint family, Lamiaceae, which includes plants associated with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antiseptic properties.The plant can grow to approximately 1.5 metres tall, with pale blue and white flowers that resemble Argentina’s national colours. Those colours make the choice of namesake especially fitting for a footballer who represented his country across a career spanning more than two decades.The name follows botanical naming conventions, which often adapt a person’s surname into Latin. The ending “i” indicates possession, socan be understood as “Messi’s sage”.The species was described by researchers led by Paul Gonzales of the Natural History Museum at the National University of San Marcos, alongside Argentine researcher Rolando Uria and biologist Jean Capcha-Ramos of Huarango Nature. Their study appeared in the October edition of the botanical journalThe plant’s restricted range and endangered classification give the discovery significance beyond its unusual celebrity namesake. Its name may draw attention to the species, but its survival depends on protecting the mountain habitat where it grows.In May 2024, Guinness World Records recognised Messi as the footballer with the most species named after him, recording five at the time.now brings that total to six.The names span living animals, prehistoric fossils, fungi and now a flowering plant. The fossil condor and brachiopod also show that the honour is not limited to species alive today.Messi’s record is unusual, although he is not the only footballer whose name has entered scientific classification. Diego Maradona has been associated with four named organisms, but one, the fairy wasp, was later found to be the same species as an earlier-named wasp and is therefore no longer considered valid.Messi’s name has reached science through a series of researchers choosing to recognise his influence, rather than through any single award or official campaign. The latest example connects his sporting identity directly with Argentina’s colours, even though the plant itself grows across the border in Peru.The tribute also arrives after a remarkable international career. Messi made his senior Argentina debut against Hungary on 17 August 2005, briefly retired from international football in 2016, then returned to lead the team through its major successes.He captained Argentina to Copa América titles in 2021 and 2024 and the 2022 World Cup triumph in Qatar. Messi has made 208 appearances and scored 126 goals for Argentina, winning the Ballon d’Or eight times. He scored in Argentina’s 3-0 victory over Benin in his final international match earlier this month. Now 39, he continues his club career with Inter Miami and has also been nominated among the 30 contenders for the 2026 Ballon d’Or.The practice of naming newly described organisms after footballers goes back further than Messi’s record. In December 2009, researchers named 12 newly described microcaddisfly species after members of Brazil’s 1958 World Cup-winning team, including Pelé, whose name was given toMaradona’s scientific namesakes include a fossil damselfly, a parasitic fluke and a sea snail, alongside the wasp later found not to be a distinct species.For Messi, the new sage adds another entry to a record already recognised by Guinness, while also drawing attention to a plant whose future is less secure than the footballer’s place in the sport’s history. The sixth namesake may be a small botanical discovery, but it carries both a tribute and a reminder of the biodiversity researchers are still identifying.
Article Summary: Messi’s latest botanical honour takes his Guinness World Records tally to six species, including animals, fossils and fungi. A sage plant discovered in the Peruvian Andes has become the sixth species named after Lionel Messi, extending a record already shared by a lizard, spider, fossil brachiopod, condor and fungus.

The fine is tiny beside Ronaldo’s earnings, but the rules did not measure his wealth

Cristiano Ronaldo earns an estimated $300 million a year, yet Portugal’s football federation fined him just €255 for walking out of the national-team camp, alongside a 30-day suspension that was backdated. The seemingly lenient punishment has raised eyebrows, prompting questions over whether the federation went easy on its biggest star. Ronaldo, whose estimated net worth ranges between $1.2 billion and $1.4 billion, became the world’s first billionaire footballer. So, how did the federation arrive at this surprisingly small fine, and why did the suspension have little impact on Ronaldo’s international schedule?The Portuguese Football Federation’s Disciplinary Council found Ronaldo guilty of intentionally leaving national-team duties without an acceptable justification, under Article 160(1) of its disciplinary regulations. The case followed his departure from Portugal’s camp during the October international break, amid a dispute over his playing time under Jesus.The federation’s ruling imposed a 30-day suspension and an additional fine of 2.5 Units of Account, amounting to €255. The council said it had upheld the charges in full, finding that Ronaldo had committed the disciplinary offence on one occasion and intentionally.The punishment followed a provisional suspension, with the federation describing the final outcome as “adequate and sufficient”.Ronaldo admitted responsibility for leaving the camp, publicly apologised and said he would accept whatever sanction was imposed. He has also made clear that he is not ready to retire from international football and remains keen to represent Portugal.The disciplinary council also said Ronaldo had formally admitted the facts underlying the charge in a statement submitted on Friday, October 16. His confession and clean disciplinary record were among the factors that reduced the severity of the punishment.The fine was not calculated as a percentage of Ronaldo’s salary, nor was the federation required to consider his wealth when setting the amount. Its regulations use a fixed legal measure called a Unit of Account, or UC, valued at €102.Under Article 160(1), the standard financial penalty for this offence is between five and 10 UC, equivalent to €510 to €1,020. The regulation also provides for a suspension ranging from one to six months.Ronaldo’s case was assessed with mitigating circumstances, including his lack of a previous disciplinary record over his 20-plus-year international career, his full, unconditional confession to the facts underlying the charge, and his public apology to fans and teammates, expressing remorse for his actions. Under the sentencing framework described in the disciplinary materials, these factors reduced the applicable financial sanction range to 1.25–2.5 Units of Account (UC), setting the maximum fine at €255. Here’s how the rules and calculations led to that figure.The council selected the upper end of that reduced range: 2.5 UC multiplied by €102 produces exactly €255. In other words, the fine was the maximum permitted within the reduced legal limits, rather than an amount chosen simply because the federation wished to go easy on Ronaldo.The same mitigation affected his sporting punishment, although the suspension carried consequences beyond the relatively modest financial figure.The council imposed a 30-day suspension, the minimum duration described in the ruling’s adjusted range. The federation backdated the suspension to the period beginning around Ronaldo’s departure from camp, meaning much of the ban elapsed before Portugal’s next scheduled international fixture.According to the Associated Press, the suspension began on October 1, the day of Portugal’s game against Denmark. Ronaldo had already served 19 days by the time the punishment was reported, leaving him expected to be available for Portugal’s next Nations League match against Denmark on November 14.The timeline meant the suspension was unlikely to cost him an international appearance, provided the dates and eligibility assessment remained unchanged. Portugal’s federation president, Pedro Proença, has also described Ronaldo as a key player and expressed confidence that the captain would resolve his dispute with Jesus and return to the squad.The €255 penalty looks startling when compared with Ronaldo’s income. Forbes estimates that he is set to earn around $300 million in 2026, including approximately $250 million from Al Nassr during the 2026–27 season and another $50 million through endorsements and business ventures.Sky Sports has reported that Ronaldo earns roughly £488,000 a day at Al Nassr, meaning he could cover the fine in about 39 seconds on those wages.For Ronaldo, €255 is barely a dent in his fortune. But the small figure has a very specific explanation: Portugal’s disciplinary rules, combined with his admission and clean record, brought the maximum permissible fine down to just 2.5 accounting units. The 30-day suspension was also backdated, meaning he would be eligible for Portugal’s next match, should he wish to rejoin the national side.
Article Summary: Cristiano Ronaldo received a €255 fine and a backdated 30-day suspension for walking out of Portugal's national team camp. The fine was not calculated as a percentage of Ronaldo’s salary, nor was the federation required to consider his wealth when setting the amount. Ronaldo earns an estimated $300 million a year. The suspension has little impact on Ronaldo's international schedule.

Article Title: OFFSIDE | Sir Alex Ferguson's new book 'Games of My Life' is a cruel time machine for Man Utd fans
Article Text:
GAMES OF MY LIFE BY ALEX FERGUSON

Games of My Life

.

Source: Games of My Life

Games of My Life by Alex Ferguson with Miichael Moritz

Source: Games of My Life

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The Golden Era of TV was littered with peak moments when one suddenly just knew that the series one was watching would remain embedded in posterity forever: when Walter “Heisenberg” White says : “Say my name”, or when Don Draper, while holding forth on nostalgia , tells a bunch of Kodak executives that their slide projector is a time machine. And for those who love dragons and incest, that peak moment came when The Rains of Castamere – the Lannister song – suddenly started playing at the Twins, signalling what posterity will remember as the Red Wedding.That dinner party was actually inspired by real history, specifically the Black Dinner of 1440 and the Massacre of Glencoe in 1692. Another gory chapter of British history was the Wars of the Roses, an internecine struggle for the English throne. In the aforementioned wars, thornier than rosier, the white rose represented Yorkshire while the red one represented Lancashire. Those colour loyalties live on to this day, with Yorkshire’s colours represented by Leeds United and, across the Pennines, Lancashire’s colours represented by Manchester United , who met recently in a Premier League encounter that could have used a few thorns.These days, the Premier League’s Game of Thrones matters about as much to Manchester United as the Iron Throne did to House Frey after Arya Stark came calling, as evidenced by Michael Carrick’s men ended up extending their winless streak to six matches against Leeds United, which really suggests that the Manchester United board should have taken one’s suggestion and stuck to simply swapping interim managers instead of appointing a full-time one.The same team that took more league points than any other club during Carrick’s interim spell last season has now had its worst start to a league season since 1986.So, with reality disappointing time and again, this week’s Offside will take a leaf from Don Draper’s playbook and peddle nostalgia, which in this case is a walk down memory lane with Sir Alex Ferguson, or rather his new book:Sir Alex, like The Beatles, is one of the most written-about entities in the world, so one would wonder what new insight one can gain from a man who has been in the public eye for decades and whose every word and deed has been scrutinised in excruciating detail.He has written numerous books, but the format is a little different this time, with Sir Alex picking 21 different games over a span of 70 years, and it’s a list so storied that the magical night in Barcelona doesn’t make the cut.There’s the first time he lifted a cup as a 13-year-old for Govan High School, falling in love with the Beautiful Game after watching Real Madrid beat Eintracht Frankfurt 7-3 at Hampden Park in Glasgow, and the hat-trick for St Johnstone that stopped him from taking a leaf from a popular Bollywood actor and emigrating to Canada to become a toolmaker.Some choices are obvious, like the afternoon his Aberdeen thrashed Hibernian 5-0 to break the Old Firm duopoly of Scottish football and win the Scottish league title.There’s Manchester United’s 1992 defeat to Liverpool that ensured Leeds would become league champions, and the 1-0 defeat of Crystal Palace, during which Dion Dublin broke his leg, leaving Sir Alex in need of a striker. He looked across the Pennines to sign a mercurial Frenchman who would change the destiny of Manchester United and the Premier League.There are two matches against Bolton that stand out for different reasons.The first is in 1995, when Sir Alex sold off many of his top stars and replaced them with youngsters named Beckham, Scholes and Giggs, vindicating his faith in youth. Then there’s a 2007 match against Bolton again, this time signalling the coming of age of Wayne Rooney and Cristiano Ronaldo.Others are more emotional, like his first match back at Old Trafford after suffering a brain haemorrhage that nearly killed him, left him temporarily unable to speak and made him fear for his future, or the 2024 FA Cup final against Man City when Kobbie Mainoo scored the winner, which remains Manchester United’s last trophy.Many of the matches lead into very deep tangents. After all, everyone knows Beckham, Giggs, Scholes, the Nevilles and Butt, but few have heard how the troika of coaches shaped them: Eric Harrison, the youth team coach, Nobby Stiles and Bryan Kidd, who helped mould those youngsters.Sir Alex himself was shaped by a similar upbringing in Govan, the working-class district of Glasgow where his father worked in the shipyards along the River Clyde. He credits his mother Elizabeth with giving him confidence and his father Alexander with instilling his relentless drive to succeed. The latter was a hard taskmaster who would find fault even when his son scored a hat-trick. There were other influences, including Johnny Borland of the Boys' Brigade and Mr Symington, his school coach, who demanded punctuality and discipline. Long before the famous hairdryer treatment became part of footballing folklore, a young Alex was learning that talent without discipline would only get you so far.Perhaps the most interesting choice is the 1999 Champions League semi-final against Juventus, where Roy Keane produced what Sir Alex considers his greatest performance in a Manchester United shirt. Keane and Sir Alex are no longer on talking terms after the former went full Roy Keane during an MUTV broadcast, but the remarkable tribute, considering how acrimoniously things ended between the two men, is a reminder that even the most bitter personal disagreements cannot completely erase the memory of a footballing genius.Then there's the final game of his managerial career, a ridiculous 5-5 draw against West Bromwich Albion. For a man who spent nearly three decades demanding discipline, organisation and control, it was a hilariously chaotic way to sign off. Sir Alex had managed 1,500 games for Manchester United, won 13 Premier League titles and conquered Europe twice, and somehow his final act was to watch a team he had built concede five goals to West Brom.There are gentler memories too. In 2014, Sir Alex watched his son Darren lead Peterborough United to victory over Chesterfield in the Johnstone's Paint Trophy final at Wembley. A man who had won practically every major honour available to an English club was now watching his son win a competition that barely registers in the wider footballing consciousness. Yet there it was, among the 21 most important matches of his life. Perhaps there are some victories that mean considerably more when you're watching from the stands.And then there's Scotland's 2021 victory over Israel, which finally resolved one of Sir Alex's lingering regrets. Despite having conquered English football, won European trophies and received a knighthood, he had never been officially awarded a Scotland cap. He had actually represented his country on a tour in 1967, but those appearances had not been recognised as full internationals. It took 54 years for the Scottish FA to correct the anomaly, and Sir Alex finally received his cap at Hampden Park in October 2021, aged 79.For a man who had won almost everything football had to offer, that small blue-and-gold cap remained a matter of immense Scottish pride. The winning goal that evening, appropriately enough, came from Scott McTominay, another young footballer who had emerged from the Manchester United academy.One realises while reading the book that the most memorable moments of a life rarely follow the hierarchy imposed by history books. The footballing world will forever remember the Treble, the great rivalries and the astonishing collection of silverware, but Sir Alex remembers a schoolboy cup final, his son winning at Wembley and a Scotland cap that arrived more than half a century late. At times, it’s obvious that the man who shaped modern football discourse felt greatly for the fan who had no say in his team’s fortunes, something Sir Alex has also had to contend with in his latter days.And perhaps that's why the book is such a delightful read for Manchester United fans of a certain vintage, particularly those of us who grew up believing that winning the Premier League was almost a constitutional right. One watched the club lift trophies with the casual entitlement of a hereditary monarch, blissfully unaware that the dynasty would someday end and the heirs would spend the next decade fighting over the furniture.Sadly, life is not a Don Draper client pitch and there’s no return to the Golden Era.There’s no time machine. There’s no going back to, say, a pre-COVID world where generative AI didn’t ruin anything. Nostalgia is wonderful, but it comes with a sell-by date. Watching highlights of the glorious European nights and the Fergie-time winners, or remembering what it felt like to watch a group of youngsters dominate the Premier League, won’t change the present.United fans of my vintage joke that our adult lives comprise paying for the joys of the magical United nights of our childhood. Perhaps the mediocrity of adulthood is the price we are paying for the joys of our childhood.The great French philosopher who played a little football once said: “When seagulls follow the trawler, it’s because they think sardines will be thrown into the sea.” Today, we are the seagulls following the trawler, sifting through the sardines of nostalgia because the truth is that Sir Alex is now 84, most of his fledglings are annoying voices on podcasts, the Theatre of Dreams is now the Theatre of Predictable Disappointments and Manchester United can’t even string together enough wins to let a content creator get a haircut.
Article Summary: Sir Alex Ferguson has written a new book, Games of My Life. The former Manchester United boss picks 21 games over a span of 70 years. Sir Alex picks matches against Bolton, Leeds and Liverpool. He also picks his first match back at Old Trafford after suffering brain haemorrhage.

Article Title: Cristiano Ronaldo punished for Portugal camp walkout: 30-day suspension and fine after clash with Jorge Jesus
Article Text:
Portugal's Cristiano Ronaldo (AP Photo)

Rift with coach sparks dramatic exit

Suspension backdated, Ronaldo set for return

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Cristiano Ronaldo's decision to walk out of Portugal's national team camp following a reported disagreement with coach Jorge Jesus has cost the superstar forward a 30-day suspension and a fine of €255 ($285), with the Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) describing the punishment as “adequate and sufficient”.The FPF announced the disciplinary decision on Monday, confirming that the 41-year-old had admitted the facts underlying the charges in a formal statement submitted on Friday. His admission and clean disciplinary record were considered mitigating circumstances, helping reduce the sanction. The fine was the maximum permitted after those circumstances were taken into account.Ronaldo, who had already apologised for his actions and acknowledged that he deserved to be punished, can appeal the decision. The Portugal captain had not immediately reacted publicly to the announcement.The controversy erupted during Portugal's recent Nations League campaign after Ronaldo was left on the bench for the team's match against Norway on September 27. Portugal won the game 2-1, but the forward was reportedly frustrated after being left unused despite believing that Jesus had assured him he would feature for around 30 minutes.Ronaldo also accused the coach of breaking a second agreement to publicly explain the situation. Jesus denied making any such promises but left the door open for the forward's return after the match.The disagreement escalated when Ronaldo left Portugal's training camp ahead of the subsequent Nations League fixture against Denmark. The Portuguese Football Federation subsequently initiated disciplinary proceedings over the incident, with the case formally opened in October.The federation's disciplinary council found that Ronaldo had intentionally committed an offence under Article 160(1) of its disciplinary regulations. The player had also apologised for failing to acknowledge supporters after the Norway match and for leaving his teammates, while accepting that his conduct could not go unpunished.Despite the disciplinary action, Ronaldo is expected to be available for Portugal's next Nations League fixture against Denmark on November 14. The suspension began on October 1, the day of the Denmark match, allowing the forward to serve a substantial portion of the 30-day punishment before his anticipated return.Portugal managed to progress in the Nations League without their captain, registering victories over Denmark and Norway after the controversy. The results helped the side secure qualification for the quarter-finals.FPF president Pedro Proenca has also indicated that the federation wants Ronaldo back in the national setup once the matter is resolved.The relatively modest financial penalty is unlikely to be the main consequence for the Al-Nassr forward. Instead, the suspension serves as a disciplinary reminder that even Portugal's most prominent player is subject to the federation's rules, regardless of his standing in the national side.
Article Summary: Cristiano Ronaldo has been handed a 30-day suspension and a fine of €255 ($285) Ronaldo left Portugal's national team camp after a reported disagreement with coach Jorge Jesus. The Portugal captain is expected to be available for Portugal's next Nations League fixture against Denmark on November 14.
